newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-IRABU MEETS PRESS, DONS YANKEE PINSTRIPES.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-IRABU MEETS PRESS, DONS YANKEE PINSTRIPES.

text.p: Japanese pitching star Hideki Irabu Friday called his opportunity to play for the New York Yankees a precious thing and said he hoped to help bring New York another championship.

After months of battling to acquire the rights to the right-hander and weeks of trying to sign the man touted as the Japanese Nolan Ryan, the Yankees Thursday announced that Irabu had signed a four-year deal believed to be worth $12.8 million and trotted him out for the media on Friday.

"This is big for the Yankees and all of us who have been involved in this pursuit," said Yankees vice president of player development and scouting Mark Newman. "We have acquired one of the finest young pitchers in the world."
"My first goal or dream was to wear a Yankee pinstripe uniform," said Irabu through an interpretor. "I want to do my best to contribute to the team to win another championship."

With Irabu agreeing to terms, the Yankees send the San Diego Padres $3 million in cash, outfielder Ruben Rivera and minor-league pitcher Rafael Medina. In addition to Irabu, New York receives minor-leaguers Homer Bush, Gordon Amerson and a player to be named.
The negotiations went down to the wire with the deal contingent upon the Yankees being able to sign Irabu to a contract by Saturday.
"The New York Yankees are a very special team, they have the pinstripes tradition. It's an honour to draw on a Yankees uniform," said the 27-year-old Irabu.

Standing behind a podium with his interpreter seated to his left, Irabu showed almost no emotion throughout the proceedings until he donned a Yankees jersey and cap for the cameras and broke into a huge grin.

The Padres owned the rights to Irabu as a result of their agreement with his Japanese team, the Chiba Lotte Marines. But Irabu was steadfast in his desire to pitch only for the Yankees and was prepared to sit out the entire season if he was not traded to New York.
Irabu said he was happy to put all of that behind him and finally get back to baseball with the defending World Series champions.
"Rather than think of the pressure and negative aspects, I'm really happy than I can get on the mound and pitch again," he said.

"I would like to treat this opportunity as a precious thing and do my best," said Irabu, who added that he received some advice about pitching in the major leagues from Los Angeles Dodgers Japanes ace Hideo Nomo.
Irabu will become the fourth Japanese player in the major leagues, joining three other pitchers -- Nomo, Shigetoshi Hasegawa of the Anaheim Angels and Takashi Kashiwada of the New York Mets.
It is believed that Irabu received the biggest contract ever for a player who has never played in the majors.
"This young man will do fine," predicted Yankees owner George Steinbrenner.
"He has a chance to be great and it's a giant step in internationalizing baseball."

Irabu, who led the Japanese Pacific League with a 2.40 ERA last season and has 1,111 strikeouts in 1,101 2/3 innings pitched, will head to Tampa to work out in the Yankees minor league system for three or four weeks.
The Yankees hope to have Irabu on the major league roster around the July All-Star break.
